'''barcarole''' (bär′ka̤-rōl), ''n.'' [< It. ''barcarolo'', ''barcaruolo'', a boatman (fem. ''barcaruola'', > F. ''barcarolle'', > E. ''barcarole'', a boatman’s song), < ''barca'', a bark, barge: see ''bark''<sup>3</sup>.] '''1.''' An Italian boatman.—'''2.''' A simple song or melody sung by Venetian gondoliers.—'''3.''' A piece of instrumental music composed in imitation of such a song.

Also spelled ''barcarolle''.

'''barce''' (bärs), ''n.'' [Another spelling of ''barse'', q. v.] An English (Yorkshire) name of the stickleback.

'''barcelona†''' (bär-sē-lō′nä̤), ''n.'' [Named from ''Barcelona'', a city in Spain.] A neck-cloth of soft silk.
{{smaller block|The author of Waverley entered; . . . a double ''barcelona'' protected his neck.
{{right|''Scott'', Peveril of the Peak, Pref.}}}}

'''barcenite''' (bär′se-nīt), ''n.'' [After Prof. Mariano ''Barcena'', of Mexico.] A hydrous antimoniate of mercury from Huitzuco, Mexico, derived from the alteration of livingstonite.

'''B. Arch.''' An abbreviation of ''Bachelor of Architecture'', a degree granted by some colleges and schools in the United States.

'''Barclayite''' (bär′klā-īt), ''n.'' Same as ''Berean'', 2.

'''barcon, barcone''' (bär′kon, bär-kō′ne), ''n.'' [< It. ''barcone'', aug. of ''barca'', a bark: see ''bark''<sup>3</sup>.] A trading-vessel used in the Mediterranean.

'''bar-cutter''' (bär′kut″ėr), ''n.'' A shearing-machine which cuts metallic bars into lengths. ''E. H. Knight.''

'''bardash†''' (bär′dash), ''n.'' [< F. ''bardache'', < Sp. ''bardaxa'' = It. ''bardascia'', < Ar. ''bardaj'', slave, captive.] A boy kept for unnatural purposes.

'''barde<sup>1</sup>''', '''barde<sup>2</sup>''', ''n.'' See ''bard<sup>1</sup>'', ''bard<sup>2</sup>''.

'''barded''' (bär′ded), ''p. a.'' [< ''bard<sup>2</sup>'' + ''-ed<sup>2</sup>''. Cf. ''barbed<sup>2</sup>''.] Furnished with or clad in armor: said of a war-horse.

'''bardelle†''' (bär-del′), ''n.'' [< OF. ''bardelle'' (= It. ''bardella''), dim. of ''barde'': see ''bard<sup>2</sup>''.] A pack-saddle made of cloth, stuffed with straw, and tied down tightly with pack-thread.

'''Bardesanism''' (bär-des′ạ-nizm), ''n.'' [< ''Bardesanes'' + ''-ism''.] The doctrinal system of the Bardesanists.

'''Bardesanist''' (bär-des′ạ-nist), ''n.'' One of the followers of Bardesanes, of Edessa, in Mesopotamia, in the second and third centuries.
{{smaller block|He is said to have taught doctrines resembling those of the Gnostic Valentinus, namely: a self-existent principle of evil; that the soul is imprisoned in the body by way of punishment; and that therefore a body was not assumed by Christ in his incarnation, and is not to be raised at the resurrection. Recent discussions have shown, however, that the true nature of his doctrines remains an open question. There are still extant Syriac hymns and prose works ascribed to Bardesanes.}}

'''Bardesanite''' (bär-des′ạ-nīt), ''n.'' [< ''Bardesanes'' + ''-ite<sup>2</sup>''.] A Bardesanist.
{{smaller block|He [Mani] looked upon what he considered to be Christianity proper, that is, Christianity as it had been developed among the sects of the Basilidians, Marcionites, and perhaps ''Bardesanites'', as a comparatively valuable and sound religion.
{{right|''Encyc. Brit.'', XV. 485.}}}}

'''bardic''' (bär′dik), ''a.'' [< ''bard<sup>1</sup>'' + ''-ic''.] Of, pertaining to, or of the character of a bard or bards.

'''barding''' (bär′ding), ''n.'' [< ''bard''<sup>2</sup> + ''-ing''<sup>1</sup>.] Horse-armor in general: usually in the plural. See ''bard''<sup>2</sup>, 1.

'''bardish''' (bär′dish), ''a.'' [< ''bard''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ish''<sup>1</sup>.] Pertaining to or characteristic of bards: as, “''bardish'' impostures,” ''Selden'', Drayton’s Polyolbion.

'''bardism''' (bär′dizm), ''n.'' [< ''bard''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ism''.] The science of bards; bardic principles or methods.

'''bardlet''' (bärd′let), ''n.'' [< ''bard''<sup>1</sup> + ''-let''.] A bardling.

'''bardling''' (bärd′ling), ''n.'' [< ''bard''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ling''<sup>1</sup>.] An inferior bard; a mediocre or inexperienced poet.
{{smaller block|The forte of ''bardlings'' is the foible of a bard.
{{right|''Stedman'', Poets of America, p. 169.}}}}

'''bardocucullus''' (bär″dō-kū-kul′us), ''n.''; pl. ''bardocuculli'' (-ī). [NL.] A kind of cowled cloak anciently worn by some Gallic peasants, and adopted by Romans and monks. See ''cucullus''.

'''bards''' (bärdz), ''n.'' [Sc.; cf. F. ''barbote'', an eelpout.] A local name in Edinburgh of the eelpout, ''Zoarces viviparus''.

'''bardship''' (bärd′ship), ''n.'' [< ''bard''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ship''.] The office of bard; position or standing as a bard.
{{smaller block|The Captain . . . showed a particular respect for my ''bardship''.
{{right|''Burns'', Border Tour, p. 569. (''N. E. D.'')}}}}

{{c|{{smaller|Barbel (''Barbus vulgaris'').}}}}
''B. vulgaris'': used with varying latitude by different writers.

'''barbute†''', ''n.''   [OF., orig. fem. of *''barbut'', ''barbu'', mod. F. ''barbu'', bearded, < ''barbe'', beard.]   '''1.''' A steel cap without vizor, but covering the cheeks and ears, used in the fifteenth century and later by foot-soldiers, archers, etc., and by the common people in times of danger.—'''2.''' A man-at-arms: from the name of the helmet worn by heavily armed men.

'''barca<sup>1</sup>''' (bär′kä̤), ''n.'' A fish of the family ''Ophiocephalidæ'' (''Ophiocephalus barca''), living in the fresh waters of Bengal.

'''barca<sup>2</sup>''' (bär′kä̤), ''n.''   [It., Sp., bark: see ''bark''<sup>3</sup>.]   A boat, skiff, or barge.   ''N. E. D.''—'''Barca longa''' {{smaller|(lit. long boat), a fishing-boat, common in the Mediterranean.   ''Fincham'', Ship-building, iv. 11.}}

'''Barcan''' (bär′kan), ''a.'' Of or pertaining to Barca, a vilayet of the Turkish empire, in northern Africa, lying to the north of the Libyan desert, and between Egypt and the gulf of Sidra.
{{smaller block|Take the wings}}
<poem>Of morning, pierce the ''Barcan'' wilderness.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Bryant'', Thanatopsis.}}}}

'''barcarole''' (bär′ka̤-rōl), ''n.''   [< It. ''barcarolo'', ''barcaruolo'', a boatman (fem. ''barcaruola'', > F. ''barcarolle'', > E. ''barcarole'', a boatman’s song), < ''barca'', a bark, barge: see ''bark''<sup>3</sup>.]   '''1.''' An Italian boatman.—'''2.''' A simple song or melody sung by Venetian gondoliers.—'''3.''' A piece of instrumental music composed in imitation of such a song.

Also spelled ''barcarolle''.

'''barce''' (bärs), ''n.''   [Another spelling of ''barse'', q. v.]   An English (Yorkshire) name of the stickleback.

'''barcelona†''' (bär-sē-lō′nä̤), ''n.''   [Named from ''Barcelona'', a city in Spain.]   A neck-cloth of soft silk.
{{smaller block|The author of Waverley entered; . . . a double ''barcelona'' protected his neck.
{{right|''Scott'', Peveril of the Peak, Pref.}}}}

'''barcenite''' (bär′se-nīt), ''n.''   [After Prof. Mariano ''Barcena'', of Mexico.]   A hydrous antimoniate of mercury from Huitzuco, Mexico, derived from the alteration of livingstonite.

'''B. Arch.''' An abbreviation of ''Bachelor of Architecture'', a degree granted by some colleges and schools in the United States.

'''Barclayite''' (bär′klā-īt), ''n.'' Same as ''Berean'', 2.

'''barcon, barcone''' (bär′kon, bär-kō′ne), ''n.''   [< It. ''barcone'', aug. of ''barca'', a bark: see ''bark''<sup>3</sup>.]   A trading-vessel used in the Mediterranean.

'''bar-cutter''' (bär′kut″ėr), ''n.'' A shearing-machine which cuts metallic bars into lengths.   ''E. H. Knight.''

'''bard<sup>1</sup>''' (bärd), ''n.''   [Formerly also ''barth'', ''bardh'' (< W.), and Sc. ''baird'' (< Gael.); = F. ''barde'' = Sp. Pg. It. ''bardo'', < LL. ''bardus'', Gr. βάρδος; of Celtic origin: W. ''bardd'' = Ir. and Gael. ''bard'' = Corn. ''bardh'' = Bret. ''barz'', a poet.]   '''1.''' A poet and singer among the ancient Celts; one whose occupation was to compose and sing verses in honor of the heroic achievements of princes and brave men, and on other subjects, generally to the accompaniment of the harp. {{smaller|The Welsh bards formed a hereditary order regulated by laws, and held stated festivals for competition, called ''eisteddfods'', which after a long suspension were revived in the eighteenth century. (See ''eisteddfod''.) There was also a hereditary gild of bards in Ireland, many of whom attained great skill.}}
{{smaller block|There is amongest the Irish a certayne kind of people called ''Bards'', which are to them insteede of poetts, whose profession is to sett foorth the prayses and disprayses of men in theyr poems and rimes. {{right|''Spenser'', State of Ireland.}}}}
'''2†.''' Formerly, in Scotland, a strolling musician; a minstrel: classed with vagabonds, as an object of penal laws.
{{smaller block|All vagabundis, fulis [fools], ''bardis'', scudlaris, and siclike idill pepill, sall be brint in the cheek.
{{right|''Kenneth’s Stat.'', in Sir J. Balfour’s Practick, 680. (''N. E. D.'')}}}}
'''3.''' In modern use, a poet: as, the ''bard'' of Avon (Shakspere); the Ayrshire ''bard'' (Burns).
{{smaller block|<poem>''Bard'', who with some diviner art
Hast touched the ''bard’s'' true lyre, a nation’s heart.</poem>
{{right|''Lowell'', To Lamartine.}}}}
'''4.''' [See def. 2 and ''bardy'', and cf. ''skald'', ''scald'', a poet, as related to ''scold''.] A scold: applied only to women. [Shetland.]

'''bard<sup>2</sup>''' (bärd), ''n.''   [Also corruptly ''barb''<sup>2</sup>, formerly ''barde'', < F. ''barde'' (= It. Sp. Pg. ''barda''), the {{img float|file=century v01 p0476 c2f1.png|width=228px|align=right|cap={{smaller|Horse-armor of Maximilian I. of Germany. ''a'', chamfron; ''b'', crinière; ''c'', poitrel; ''d'', croupière, or buttock-piece.}}}} trappings of a horse, the defensive armor of a war-horse. Cf. OF. ''bardelle'' (see ''bardelle''), F. dial. ''aubarde'', Sp. Pg. ''albarda'', a pack-saddle, < Ar. ''al-barda’ah'', < ''al'', the, + ''barda’ah'', a pad of wool placed under a saddle, a pack-saddle. But the meaning seems to have been influenced by Icel. ''bardh'', the beak or prow of a ship of war, the brim of a helmet, orig. a beard, = E. ''beard'' (see ''beard''); hence the variations of form, ''barde'' and ''barbe''.]   '''1.''' Any one of the pieces of defensive armor used in medieval Europe to protect the horse. {{smaller|There is no record of any general use of such armor in antiquity or among Oriental peoples, or in the European middle ages before the fifteenth century. Housings of different kinds of stuff, sometimes quilted and wadded in exposed parts, the saddle with its appurtenances, and occasionally a chamfron, were all the defense provided for horses until that time. The piece of armor most commonly used after the chamfron (which see) was the bard of the breast. See ''poitrel.'' The croupière, or part covering the haunches, was added at the close of the fifteenth century; but after the wars of the Roses the bards reached their fullest development, and the upper part of the body of the horse was covered as completely with steel as the body of his rider. See ''croupière.''}}
Hence—'''2.''' ''pl.'' The housings of a horse, used in tourneys, justs, and processions during the later middle ages. They were most commonly of stuff woven or embroidered with the arms of the rider.
{{smaller block|The bases and ''bardes'' of their horse were grene sattyn.
{{right|''Hall'', Henry VIII., an. 1 (1548).}}}}
'''3.''' ''pl.'' Armor of metal plates, worn in the sixteenth century and later. See ''armor''.
{{smaller block|A compleat French man-at-armes with all his ''bards.''
{{right|''Florio'', tr. of Montaigne, II. ix. 225. (''N. E. D.'')}}}}

'''bard<sup>2</sup>''' (bärd), ''v. t.''   [< ''bard<sup>2</sup>'', ''n.'']   To caparison with bards, as a horse; to furnish or accoutre with armor, as a man.
{{smaller block|Fifteen hundred men . . . ''barded'' and richly trapped.
{{right|''Stow'', Edw. IV., an. 1474.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Above the foaming tide, I ween,
Scarce half the charger’s neck was seen;
For he was ''barded'' from counter to tail,
And the rider was armed complete in mail.</poem>
{{right|''Scott'', L. of L. M., i. 29.}}}}

'''bard<sup>3</sup>''' (bärd), ''n.''   [< F. ''barde'' (= Pg. ''barda'' = Sp. ''albarda''), a strip of bacon; a particular use of ''barde'', trappings: see ''bard<sup>2</sup>''.]   A strip of bacon used to cover a fowl or meat in roasting.

'''bard<sup>3</sup>''' (bärd), ''v. t.''   [< ''bard<sup>3</sup>'', ''n.'']   To cover with thin bacon, as a bird or meat to be roasted.

'''bardash†''' (bär′dash), ''n.''   [< F. ''bardache'', < Sp. ''bardaxa'' = It. ''bardascia'', < Ar. ''bardaj'', slave, captive.]   A boy kept for unnatural purposes.

'''barde<sup>1</sup>''', '''barde<sup>2</sup>''', ''n.'' See ''bard<sup>1</sup>'', ''bard<sup>2</sup>''.

'''barded''' (bär′ded), ''p. a.''   [< ''bard<sup>2</sup>'' + ''-ed<sup>2</sup>''. Cf. ''barbed<sup>2</sup>''.]   Furnished with or clad in armor: said of a war-horse.

'''bardelle†''' (bär-del′), ''n.''   [< OF. ''bardelle'' (= It. ''bardella''), dim. of ''barde'': see ''bard<sup>2</sup>''.]   A pack-saddle made of cloth, stuffed with straw, and tied down tightly with pack-thread.

'''Bardesanism''' (bär-des′ạ-nizm), ''n.''   [< ''Bardesanes'' + ''-ism''.]   The doctrinal system of the Bardesanists.

'''Bardesanist''' (bär-des′ạ-nist), ''n.'' One of the followers of Bardesanes, of Edessa, in Mesopotamia, in the second and third centuries.
{{smaller block|He is said to have taught doctrines resembling those of the Gnostic Valentinus, namely: a self-existent principle of evil; that the soul is imprisoned in the body by way of punishment; and that therefore a body was not assumed by Christ in his incarnation, and is not to be raised at the resurrection. Recent discussions have shown, however, that the true nature of his doctrines remains an open question. There are still extant Syriac hymns and prose works ascribed to Bardesanes.}}

'''Bardesanite''' (bär-des′ạ-nīt), ''n.''   [< ''Bardesanes'' + ''-ite<sup>2</sup>''.]   A Bardesanist.
{{smaller block|He [Mani] looked upon what he considered to be Christianity proper, that is, Christianity as it had been developed among the sects of the Basilidians, Marcionites, and perhaps ''Bardesanites'', as a comparatively valuable and sound religion.
{{right|''Encyc. Brit.'', XV. 485.}}}}

'''bardic''' (bär′dik), ''a.''   [< ''bard<sup>1</sup>'' + ''-ic''.]   Of, pertaining to, or of the character of a bard or bards. {{smaller block|Here, in the open air — in “the eye of light and the face of the sun,” to use the ''bardic'' style — the decrees were pronounced, and the Druids harangued the people.
{{right|''I. D’Israeli'', Amen. of Lit., I. 20.}}}}

'''barding''' (bär′ding), ''n.''   [< ''bard''<sup>2</sup> + ''-ing''<sup>1</sup>.]   Horse-armor in general: usually in the plural. See ''bard''<sup>2</sup>, 1.

'''bardish''' (bär′dish), ''a.''   [< ''bard''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ish''<sup>1</sup>.]   Pertaining to or characteristic of bards: as, “''bardish'' impostures,” ''Selden'', Drayton’s Polyolbion.

'''bardism''' (bär′dizm), ''n.''   [< ''bard''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ism''.]   The science of bards; bardic principles or methods.

'''bardlet''' (bärd′let), ''n.''   [< ''bard''<sup>1</sup> + ''-let''.]   A bardling.

'''bardling''' (bärd′ling), ''n.''   [< ''bard''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ling''<sup>1</sup>.]   An inferior bard; a mediocre or inexperienced poet.
{{smaller block|The forte of ''bardlings'' is the foible of a bard.
{{right|''Stedman'', Poets of America, p. 169.}}}}

'''bardocucullus''' (bär″dō-kū-kul′us), ''n.''; pl. ''bardocuculli'' (-ī).   [NL.]   A kind of cowled cloak anciently worn by some Gallic peasants, and adopted by Romans and monks. See ''cucullus''.

'''bards''' (bärdz), ''n.''   [Sc.; cf. F. ''barbote'', an eelpout.]   A local name in Edinburgh of the eelpout, ''Zoarces viviparus''.

'''bardship''' (bärd′ship), ''n.''   [< ''bard''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ship''.]   The office of bard; position or standing as a bard.
{{smaller block|The Captain . . . showed a particular respect for my ''bardship''.
{{right|''Burns'', Border Tour, p. 569. (''N. E. D.'')}}}}

'''bardy''' (bär′di), ''a.''   [< ''bard''<sup>1</sup>, in the depreciative senses (defs. 2 and 4), + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.]   Bold-faced; defiant; audacious. [Scotch.]

'''bare'''<sup>1</sup> (bãr), ''a.''   [< ME. ''bare'', ''bar'', < AS. ''bær'' = OS. ''bar'' = OFries. ''ber'' = D. ''baar'' = OHG. MHG. ''bar'', G. ''bar'', ''baar'' = Icel. ''berr'' = Sw. Dan. ''bar'' = OBulg. ''bosŭ'' = Lith. ''basus'', ''bosus'', bare; orig. meaning prob. ‘shining’; cf. Skt. √ ''bhās'', shine.]   '''1.''' Naked; without covering: as, ''bare'' arms; the trees are ''bare''.
{{smaller block|Thou wast naked and ''bare''. {{right|Ezek. xvi. 7.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Envy finds
More food in cities than on mountains ''bare''.</poem>
{{right|''Lowell'', Dara.}}}}
'''2.''' With the head uncovered. {{smaller|In numismatic descriptions, said of a head on a coin or medal when uncovered or devoid of any adornment, such as a diadem or laurel-wreath.}}
{{smaller block|When once thy foot enters the church, be ''bare''.
{{right|''Herbert'', Church Porch.}}}}
{{smaller block|Thou standest ''bare'' to him now, workest for him.
{{right|''Burton'', Anat. of Mel., p. 357.}}}}
'''3.''' Open to view; unconcealed; undisguised.
{{smaller block|''Bare'' in thy guilt, how foul must thou appear!
{{right|''Milton'', S. A., l. 902.}}}}
'''4.''' Lacking in appropriate covering or equipment; unfurnished: as, ''bare'' walls.—'''5†.''' Plain; simple; unadorned; without polish.
{{smaller block|Yet was their manners then but ''bare'' and plain.
{{right|''Spenser.''}}}}
'''6.''' Threadless; napless.
{{smaller block|<poem>It appears, by their ''bare'' liveries,
That they live by your bare words.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', T. G. of V., ii. 4.}}}}
'''7.''' Poor; destitute; indigent; empty; unfurnished; unprovided with what is necessary or comfortable: absolutely or with ''of''.
{{smaller block|I have made Esau ''bare''. {{right|Jer. xlix. 10.}}}}
{{smaller block|Upon her death, when her nearest friends thought her very ''bare'', her executors found in her strong box about £150 in gold. {{right|''Swift'', Death of Stella.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Tho’ your violence should leave them ''bare''
''Of'' gold and silver, swords and darts remain.</poem>
{{right|''Dryden'', tr. of Juvenal’s Satires.}}}}
'''8.''' Empty; valueless; paltry; worthless.
{{smaller block|<poem>Not what we give, but what we share—
For the gift without the giver is ''bare''.</poem>
{{right|''Lowell'', Sir Launfal.}}}}
'''9.''' Mere; scarcely or just sufficient: as, the ''bare'' necessaries of life; a ''bare'' subsistence.
{{smaller block|<poem>Pray you, cast off these fellows, as unfitting
For your ''bare'' knowledge, and far more your company.</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Scornful Lady, iv. 2.}}}}
'''10.''' Unaccompanied; without addition; simple.
{{smaller block|It was a ''bare'' petition of a state. {{right|''Shak.'', Cor., v. 1.}}}}
'''11.''' Unadorned; without literary or artistic effect; bald; meager.
{{smaller block|Much has yet to be done to make even the ''bare'' annals of the time coherent. {{right|''Athenæum'', No. 3067, p. 170.}}}}
'''12.''' In ''beer-making'', not completely covered by the bubbles formed in fermentation: said of the surface of beer.—'''13†.''' Raw; excoriated.
{{smaller block|<poem>How many flyes in whottest sommers day
Do seize upon some beast, whose flesh is ''bare''.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., VI. xi. 48.}}}}
'''14†.''' Lean; spare.<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
